items.title: 2.10 Electronic configuration and the formation of semiconductors

source_refs.note: Topic 2.10, printed pages 41-42: semiconductors and doping (Figure 2.17).

blocks.text: Semiconductors are materials that conduct electricity under some conditions; they are used in many electronic devices, including smartphones, laptops and cars. Silicon, germanium and arsenic are elements that can act as semiconductors, and semiconductors can be made because of the unique electronic configuration of these elements. Silicon (Z = 14) has the configuration 2, 8, 4, so four electrons in its valence shell. In the pure crystalline form each silicon atom is bonded to four other silicon atoms, and in this form there is no possibility of electronic conduction through the crystal.

P-type and N-type semiconductors are formed by doping a pure semiconductor with impurity atoms. Adding trivalent impurities such as boron or aluminium creates a P-type semiconductor, while adding pentavalent impurities such as phosphorus or arsenic creates an N-type. The difference lies in whether the impurity creates holes, positive charge carriers, in the lattice (P-type) or extra electrons, negative charge carriers (N-type).

blocks.alt: Three small square lattices of blue silicon atoms joined by lines with dots for bonding electron pairs. The first is pure. In the second a red aluminium atom sits in the middle with an empty circle marked hole. In the third a green phosphorus atom sits in the middle with an extra green dot marked extra electron. A box below explains doping.
blocks.caption: Pure silicon and its doping to p-type and n-type semiconductors (original schematic after Figures 2.17 and 2.18).
blocks.long_description: In pure silicon every atom shares its four valence electrons in four bonds, so no electron is free and the crystal does not conduct. Replacing a silicon atom with a trivalent atom such as aluminium leaves one bond short, a hole that behaves as a positive carrier: a p-type semiconductor. Replacing it with a pentavalent atom such as phosphorus leaves a fifth electron free as a negative carrier: an n-type semiconductor. Either conducts when connected to an external source.
